claims.claim: DMBOK2 frames data governance as authority and control over data management, establishing decision rights over data.
claims.source: GCcollab wiki 'Data Governance' citing DMBOK2 section 3.1, and summaries of DMBOK2 chapter 3, seen through search results, November 2026.

claims.claim: Policy, standard and procedure as three levels of rules, and the steward, owner, council escalation path, are common governance practice, not quotations from DMBOK2.
claims.source: General practice. Not attributed to a specific DMBOK2 passage.

concept_html:
Governance and management are different jobs. Data governance decides and oversees: who may decide what, which rules apply, and whether they are followed. Data management does the work: builds the pipelines, runs the quality checks, grants the access. DMBOK2 frames governance as setting decision rights over data. A platform team that both writes the rules and marks its own work has no oversight.

Start with decision rights. For each kind of decision, name who decides:

  • what a term means, such as "active employee" or "regretted leaver"
  • who may see a field, such as salary or a performance rating
  • what quality threshold a dataset must meet before it is published
  • whether a new use of data goes ahead

Then write the rules at three levels:

  • A policy says what must be true, and why. "Access to performance data follows the principle of least privilege."
  • A standard makes it measurable. "Ratings are masked for every role except HR business partners and the employee's own line chain."
  • A procedure says how. "Request access through the form. The data owner approves within five working days."

Policies change rarely and need senior sign-off. Standards change when the platform does. Procedures change often.

Finally, an escalation path. Most issues end with a data steward. Those that cross domains, or set precedent, go to the data owner, then to a governance council. Each decision is written down in a decision log (lesson B18-L3), so the next person finds the reason, not only the rule.

GOV-02 in your EY role plan turns these rights into a RACI.

policy: POL-07 least privilege for performance data

notes.html: One named decider per kind of decision.
The standard makes the policy testable.
A fixed path, so disputes end with a decision.

example.takeaway_html: Separate deciding from doing. Name a decider for each kind of decision, write rules as policy, standard and procedure, and log each decision with its reason.

title: Governance at the hub, decision rights, policies and escalation
why_html: Two directors argued for a quarter over whether contractors counted in "headcount". The data team changed the dashboard each time one of them complained. Nobody had the right to decide, so the definition flipped four times and trust in every people report fell. A named decision owner and one log entry settled it in a week.
